name: Water loading / hydration maxxing

angle.text: Users drink large amounts of water in the belief that it plumps skin and reduces facial puffiness. It is a common fixture of skincare and depuffing routines. Fixed targets such as eight glasses are not backed by research, and the appearance effect specifically is largely anecdotal.

summary: Drinking large amounts of water for skin and depuffing: fixed targets like eight glasses lack scientific basis, and excess carries hyponatremia risk.
note: Excessive water intake can cause hyponatremia.
currentQuick:
Water loading, or hydration maxxing, is drinking large volumes of water in pursuit of clearer skin and less facial puffiness. It is a common wellness and looksmaxxing habit.
Wikipedia describes the 'eight glasses a day' advice as unscientific and says thirst is a better guide than a fixed amount. The sources reviewed do not discuss skin hydration effects.
How it works: Believers say hydration plumps skin and flushes retained water. The sources reviewed do not cover a skin mechanism.
Risks and caveats: Drinking too much water too quickly causes hyponatremia, which Wikipedia says can cause death in minutes or hours.
deepLead:
Water loading, sometimes called hydration maxxing, is the practice of deliberately drinking large quantities of water in the belief that it improves skin or reduces puffiness.
US Adequate Intake for total water, including food, is 4.0 L a day for men and 3.0 L for women, and EFSA recommends 2.0 L for women and 2.5 L for men. Wikipedia describes the eight-glasses advice as unscientific and says thirst is a better guide. Excess intake can cause hyponatremia.

name: 16:8 time-restricted eating

angle.text: Users adopt a daily 8-hour eating window as a simple structure for eating less and getting leaner, which they link to a sharper face and body. Trials have measured weight and metabolic markers rather than appearance, so the look-based claims rest on that fat-loss pathway.

summary: Eat inside an eight-hour window and fast the other sixteen; the research is about weight and metabolic markers, not looks.
note: Not advised for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating-disorder histories.
currentQuick:
16:8 time-restricted eating means eating all meals within eight hours and fasting for sixteen. It is popular for fat loss and a leaner look.
Trials are small and short, mostly in overweight adults and athletes, and reviews report weight loss broadly similar to ordinary calorie restriction.
How it works: The window limits when food is eaten, which for many people reduces total calorie intake; researchers also study effects on fat oxidation and metabolic hormones.
Risks and caveats: Reported short-term effects include hunger, irritability, headaches and poor concentration. Reviews advise against it for pregnancy, youth, underweight people and those with eating disorders.
deepLead:
16:8 time-restricted eating (TRE) is a daily meal-timing pattern in which all food is eaten within an eight-hour window, leaving sixteen hours of fasting, often overnight plus part of the morning and evening. It belongs to the family of time-restricted eating, in which food is confined to a set daily window, commonly 8 to 12 hours.
In looksmaxxing and wider fitness culture it is used mainly for leanness: people adopt it to reduce body fat, sharpen facial definition and simplify eating routines. Published trials have studied it in overweight adults, endurance athletes, cyclists, dancers and resistance-trained lifters, generally in small groups over weeks to months.
Researchers describe the evidence on intermittent fasting as preliminary, with long-term effects not well studied, and reviews report that its advantage over ordinary calorie restriction is limited.

name: Alternate-day fasting

angle.text: Followers use alternate-day fasting as a route to rapid fat loss and a leaner face and physique. Trials show weight loss, comparable to ordinary calorie restriction, while appearance outcomes themselves have not been the focus of research.

summary: Fast every other day; trials show weight loss, but not clearly more than ordinary calorie cutting.
note: Not advised for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating-disorder histories.
currentQuick:
Alternate-day fasting alternates fast days (no or very few calories) with normal eating days. It is used for fat loss.
Randomized trials report meaningful weight loss and some improved health markers, with results generally comparable to daily calorie restriction.
How it works: The fast days create a large weekly calorie deficit; researchers also study metabolic switching and hormone changes.
Risks and caveats: Hunger, irritability, headaches and low energy are reported early on. It is advised against in pregnancy, youth, underweight people and those with eating disorders.
deepLead:
Alternate-day fasting (ADF) is an intermittent fasting pattern in which fast days alternate with unrestricted "feast" days. In the strict form no calories are eaten on fast days; in the modified form roughly a quarter of usual energy needs, often 0 to 500 kcal, is allowed.
It is used for weight and fat loss and is discussed in appearance communities as a route to leanness. Randomized trials in adults with obesity and in healthy non-obese people have compared it with daily calorie restriction or normal eating.
Reviews describe the evidence as preliminary: weight loss is clinically meaningful but generally not greater than with continuous calorie restriction.

name: 5:2 diet

angle.text: People use the 5:2 pattern as a flexible way to create a calorie deficit and lose fat, with the aim of a leaner physique. Studies show weight loss similar to standard dieting; appearance outcomes have not been the research focus.

summary: Eat normally five days, eat about 500 calories on two; weight loss is similar to ordinary dieting.
note: Not advised for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating-disorder histories.
currentQuick:
The 5:2 diet has people eat normally five days a week and eat very little on two non-consecutive days. It was popularised in 2012.
Trials and meta-analyses report weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction.
How it works: The two low-calorie days create a weekly energy deficit; researchers also examine effects on insulin, liver fat and adipose tissue.
Risks and caveats: Hunger, irritability and headaches are reported early. It is not recommended for pregnancy, youth, older adults, underweight people or those with eating disorders.
deepLead:
The 5:2 diet is an intermittent fasting pattern in which people eat normally for five days a week and limit intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days. It was popularised in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley after a 2012 BBC documentary.
It is used for weight loss and leanness. Randomized trials have compared it with continuous calorie restriction and with other diets, in people with obesity and with fatty liver disease.
Reviews report weight loss similar to other calorie-restriction approaches; its long-term effects remain little studied.

name: Fasting-mimicking diet

angle.text: The fasting-mimicking diet is promoted in longevity circles for slowing biological aging, which some users hope shows up as better skin and a leaner look. It has been studied for aging markers and disease risk, not for visible appearance.

summary: A five-day low-calorie cycle from Valter Longo; studied for aging markers and disease, not for looks.
note: Human appearance outcomes untested; supervision advised in pregnancy or eating disorders.
currentQuick:
The fasting-mimicking diet is a five-day plant-based, low-calorie, low-protein cycle created by Valter Longo, repeated every few months.
Human trials examine aging and disease markers and cancer-care settings; no study has tested appearance outcomes.
How it works: It aims to trigger fasting-like responses, such as lower IGF-1 and increased autophagy, without total food abstinence.
Risks and caveats: Intended as periodic, not daily. Medical supervision is advised with eating disorders, pregnancy or medical conditions.
deepLead:
The fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) is a five-day, low-calorie, low-protein, plant-based eating cycle designed to reproduce some physiological effects of water fasting while still supplying limited food. It was developed by biogerontologist Valter Longo at the University of Southern California.
Per Grokipedia, a typical cycle supplies roughly 1,000 kcal on day one and about 700 to 800 kcal on days two to five, repeated every one to six months; a commercial version, ProLon, is sold by L-Nutra, founded in 2009.
Its main research focus is aging, metabolic and disease markers rather than appearance, though it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for fat loss and skin or "longevity" aims. Human data come from a randomized trial of 100 healthy participants and studies in cancer patients; much other work is in mice.

name: Dry fasting

angle.text: Some wellness and looksmaxxing circles advocate dry fasting for rapid fat loss, a leaner face and clearer skin. Research covers religious daytime fasts such as Ramadan; the appearance claims for longer dry fasts are anecdotal.

summary: No food and no water; research covers religious daytime fasts, while longer dry fasts carry dehydration risk.
note: Complete fluid abstinence beyond daytime fasting is little studied and associated with dehydration risk.
currentQuick:
Dry fasting means going without both food and water. Studies cover religious daytime fasts such as Ramadan and the Bahá'í fast, plus one small five-day physiology study.
Online advocates cite autophagy and other benefits; these claims have not been tested for appearance.
How it works: Without fluids the body faces reduced blood volume and higher solute concentration, triggering hormones such as vasopressin and aldosterone.
Risks and caveats: Prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte losses and, without fluids, dehydration. Long dry fasts have little formal safety research.
deepLead:
Dry fasting is abstaining from both food and fluids for a period of time. It occurs in religious practice, such as daytime fasts of the Bahá'í Faith and Ramadan, and in some wellness circles that advocate longer dry fasts.
Advocates in online communities say it deepens fasting effects such as autophagy. Research on dry fasting is small and mostly examines religious daytime fasts in healthy volunteers.
Medical sources note that prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte losses, and fluid restriction adds dehydration risk; the entry is classed here as carrying high risk.

name: Bulking

angle.text: Lifters bulk to add muscle size, giving a broader, more muscular physique before a later cut. Eating a calorie surplus alongside resistance training is a well-studied route to gaining muscle, with debate centring on how much fat comes with it.

summary: Eat above maintenance to build muscle; the debate is how much fat comes along.
note: Dirty bulks add more fat; steroid use alongside bulking carries separate serious risks.
currentQuick:
Bulking is eating in a calorie surplus alongside lifting to gain muscle. Clean bulks use a small surplus; dirty bulks use a large one.
The energy-balance link to muscle growth is well established, but forum users debate whether natural lifters need it and how much fat it adds.
How it works: Surplus calories and protein provide energy and material for muscle growth under progressive resistance training.
Risks and caveats: Larger surpluses add more body fat and may require a longer cut; dirty bulking may affect cholesterol and insulin sensitivity over time.
deepLead:
Bulking is a planned phase of eating above maintenance calories, combined with resistance training, to gain muscle and body weight. It is the counterpart of cutting, in which fat is lost.
Bodybuilders traditionally bulk in the off-season and cut for contests; the length of the surplus determines how much fat accompanies muscle gain. In looksmaxxing communities bulking is discussed for building a fuller, broader frame, and also debated for its effects on leanness and the face.
Wikipedia states that the link between positive energy balance and muscle growth is well established, while noting uncertainty about how much muscle is retained through later cuts.

name: Dirty bulk

angle.text: Users dirty bulk to gain size quickly without tracking food closely, accepting extra fat that is cut afterward. It is contrasted with clean bulking, and forum posters discuss it especially among steroid users. Comparisons of the two are mostly based on lifter experience.

summary: Eating a large, loosely tracked calorie surplus to gain weight fast; quick scale gains, more fat to cut later.
note: Faster fat gain is the commonly reported trade-off; no trials compare it with lean bulking in appearance terms.
currentQuick:
A dirty bulk is a bulking approach in which a person eats a large calorie surplus without closely tracking food quality or macronutrients, often using calorie-dense foods such as burgers and fries. Bodybuilding sources describe it as producing fast weight gain, including some muscle, along with substantial body fat.
On looksmaxxing forums it is usually discussed against the "clean bulk" and is often framed as something for people using anabolic steroids or for very thin people who struggle to gain. Many users advise against it for appearance, citing facial bloating.
How it works: The method relies on a calorie surplus well above maintenance combined with resistance training. A larger surplus raises the rate of scale-weight gain, but a greater share of that gain tends to be fat, and early gains include water and glycogen.
Risks and caveats: Bodybuilding encyclopedias note that dirty bulking typically adds significant fat, requiring a harsher cut afterward, and mention possible long-term effects on cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity. No legal restrictions apply; the main caveats are fat gain and metabolic health.
deepLead:
A dirty bulk is a bulking strategy in which a person eats a large calorie surplus without carefully tracking macronutrients or food quality, often relying on calorie-dense foods such as burgers and fries. It is contrasted with a clean bulk, which uses a smaller surplus and more controlled food choices to limit fat gain.
Bodybuilding references describe dirty bulking as capable of producing rapid weight and muscle gain, but usually with significant body fat that typically calls for a more aggressive cutting phase afterward. One online encyclopedia summary gives typical surpluses of roughly 500 to 1,000 kcal per day for dirty bulking versus 250 to 500 for clean bulking, and also notes possible effects on blood lipids and insulin sensitivity, though that source has internal inconsistencies and some of its figures are weakly sourced.
In looksmaxxing communities the term appears mainly in debates over whether to gain weight quickly or slowly, with many posters prioritising a lean, defined face and therefore recommending against it.

name: Lean bulk

angle.text: Lean bulking is used to add muscle slowly while staying lean enough to keep a defined face and physique. It rests on the studied link between a calorie surplus, training and muscle gain; the exact surplus that limits fat gain is mostly lifter lore.

summary: A small calorie surplus aimed at adding muscle while limiting fat gain; slower than a dirty bulk.
note: Slower gains; forum users worry about gaining facial fat during any surplus.
currentQuick:
A lean bulk is a bulking phase using a modest calorie surplus, often described as 250 to 500 kcal per day above maintenance, with the goal of gaining muscle while adding as little fat as possible. It is the counterpart of the dirty bulk.
On looksmaxxing forums, users commonly ask whether a lean bulk will make them look fat or bloated, and how to balance muscle gain against facial leanness.
How it works: Calorie intake is set slightly above maintenance alongside progressive resistance training, with weekly weight tracking used to keep gains slow. A Grokipedia summary cites targets of about 0.25 to 0.5 kg per week and protein of 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg per day.
Risks and caveats: Slower progress and some unavoidable fat gain are the main caveats described. Early weight gain includes glycogen and water. No safety concerns specific to modest surpluses are noted in the sources.
deepLead:
A lean bulk, also called a clean bulk or lean gaining, is a muscle-building phase that uses a small calorie surplus and resistance training to gain muscle while limiting fat gain. It takes longer than a large-surplus approach but is described as more precise.
A Grokipedia summary describes a surplus of 250 to 500 kcal per day above maintenance, protein of 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg per day, and weekly weight checks to keep gains near 0.25 to 0.5 kg per week; it also says intermediates can expect roughly 3 to 6 kg of muscle per year, while noting that some of its figures conflict.
In looksmaxxing communities the term is used by people who want to add muscle without looking soft in the face. Posters ask about surplus size and whether a lean bulk will cause bloating or fat gain.

name: Cutting

angle.text: Cutting is a staple of looksmaxxing leanness advice, used to lose fat so facial bone structure and muscle definition become visible. Calorie deficit reliably reduces body fat; forum claims about how face appearance changes at low body fat are anecdotal.

summary: A calorie-deficit phase to lose fat and show muscle and bone definition; a staple of looksmaxxing leanness advice.
note: Aggressive deficits carry muscle-loss and hormonal risks, and forum questions about cutting during puberty raise additional concerns.
currentQuick:
Cutting is eating in a calorie deficit to lose body fat while trying to keep muscle. In bodybuilding it is the phase before a contest, typically lasting a few months, and it is alternated with bulking.
In looksmaxxing it is the main way users try to lower body fat for a more defined face and body. Forums include many teenagers asking how aggressive a cut can be during puberty.
How it works: Intake is set below maintenance, usually with resistance training and high protein to preserve muscle. A larger deficit speeds loss but raises the risk of losing muscle. A Grokipedia summary cites deficits of about 10 to 20 percent below maintenance and a loss rate of 0.5 to 1 percent of bodyweight per week.
Risks and caveats: Larger deficits raise the risk of muscle loss, and the same summary links prolonged low energy availability to impaired hormonal function, fatigue and mood changes. Whether the cut is worthwhile if muscle is lost is described as unclear. Posts by minors asking about extreme deficits during puberty are common on forums.
deepLead:
Cutting is a phase of eating in a net negative energy balance, a calorie deficit, to lose body fat while preserving as much muscle as possible. In competitive bodybuilding, athletes typically spend an off-season building muscle and then cut for roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest.
A larger deficit produces faster weight loss but increases the risk of losing muscle, and Wikipedia notes it is unclear whether enough lean mass can be retained for the overall process to be worthwhile. A Grokipedia summary describes typical cuts of 8 to 16 weeks, a deficit of roughly 10 to 20 percent below maintenance, weekly loss of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight, and high protein intake to protect lean mass.
In looksmaxxing communities cutting is discussed as the route to a leaner, more angular face, often within the practice called leanmaxxing. Threads concern appetite suppression, carbohydrate restriction, the effect of dropping from the teens to low body fat percentages on looks, and especially cutting during puberty.

name: Leanmaxxing

angle.text: Leanmaxxing is often the first step in looksmaxxing, aimed at revealing cheekbones and the jawline by losing body fat. Fat loss reducing facial fullness is widely observed; the exact body-fat levels cited on forums come from anecdote.

summary: Losing body fat to show facial bone structure and a sharper jawline; the most common first step in looksmaxxing.
note: Mostly about calorie deficit; very low body fat and aggressive cuts carry their own risks.
currentQuick:
Leanmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for reducing body fat to make facial features, especially the jawline and cheekbones, more defined. It is usually pursued through a calorie deficit, tracking food intake, and exercise.
Threads are common on looksmax.org, including megathreads of tips and progress reports. Users also discuss how hard it gets to go below roughly 15 percent body fat and how it compares with building muscle.
How it works: Practitioners create a calorie deficit, often by tracking intake and estimating maintenance calories, and add cardio or lifting. Some forum posts also discuss appetite-suppressing drugs or supplements.
Risks and caveats: Aggressive deficits can lead to muscle loss, low energy and hormonal effects, and posters include teenagers. Drug-assisted fat loss reported in forums carries the risks of those substances. No published studies on facial leanness and attractiveness were found in the sources examined.
deepLead:
Leanmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for lowering body fat, with the aim of revealing facial bone structure and a leaner overall look. It is discussed on looksmax.org through many threads, including motivational posts, tips, guides and progress updates.
The practice is essentially a cutting phase: users calculate daily energy needs, track calories and eat below maintenance. One long-running megathread directs readers to calorie calculators, tracking apps and a deficit below estimated maintenance, alongside encouragement to include cardio.
Posters debate it against building muscle, for example asking whether a lean, light person or a heavier, stronger one looks better, and some say it becomes difficult below about 15 percent body fat. Threads also mention drugs and supplements used for appetite control.

name: Recomp

chain: Fat loss and muscle gain together
angle.text: Recomp is used mainly by beginners and skinny-fat lifters aiming to lose fat and build muscle at once, improving shape without separate bulk and cut phases. It is studied in trained and untrained groups, while forum protocols with drugs are largely anecdotal.

summary: Body recomposition: losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time, mostly discussed for beginners and skinny-fat lifters.
note: Forum threads also discuss drug-assisted recomp, which carries separate risks.
currentQuick:
Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to lose fat and add muscle at the same time, usually by eating near maintenance with resistance training and high protein. Forum posters most often discuss it for skinny-fat people who want a leaner look without a separate bulk and cut.
Threads range from natural diet and training plans to drug-assisted approaches. Some users advise against it and recommend alternating phases instead.
How it works: Calories are held around maintenance or a slight deficit while lifting and protein intake support muscle retention or gain. Forum users calculate calorie and macro targets week by week.
Risks and caveats: The sources examined contain no clinical studies. Appetite-suppressing or fat-loss drugs mentioned alongside recomp in forums carry their own medical risks and are not endorsed here. Slow, hard-to-measure progress is the main practical caveat users cite.
deepLead:
Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to reduce body fat and build muscle at the same time, in contrast with alternating a bulk and a cut. It is discussed on looksmaxxing forums mainly in relation to skinny-fat bodies, where a person has low muscle and relatively high fat.
Posters ask for week-by-week calorie and macronutrient plans, discuss modest deficits with intermittent fasting and high protein, and debate whether recomp is a sensible approach compared with a dedicated bulk or cut. Some threads discuss using fat-loss drugs and supplements to recomp while bulking.
Bodybuilding references describe bulking and cutting as separate phases with a surplus and a deficit, and note a clean bulk aims to add muscle with little fat, an approach that overlaps with recomp ideas.

name: Mini-cut

angle.text: Lifters use mini-cuts of a few weeks to shed recent fat between bulking phases, restoring definition without a long diet. It applies the established calorie-deficit pathway to fat loss; the specific 2 to 6 week format is lifter convention.

summary: A short, aggressive calorie deficit used to drop a few pounds of fat quickly, often between bulks.
note: Short deficits mostly shed water and glycogen; faster cuts raise muscle-loss risk.
currentQuick:
A mini-cut is a brief, aggressive cutting phase, often lasting a few weeks, used to lose a limited amount of fat before returning to maintenance or a bulk.
The term is common in bodybuilding and lifting communities. Few sources describe it in detail, and no clinical studies were found.
How it works: Calories are cut more sharply than in a regular cut for a short period. A Grokipedia summary says the early weight lost is mostly water and glycogen, with about 1 to 2 percent body fat reduction.
Risks and caveats: The same summary lists a higher chance of muscle loss, fatigue and metabolic slowdown, and recommends more gradual rates for most people. Aggressive deficits are described as riskier.
deepLead:
A mini-cut is a short, aggressive cutting phase in which a lifter eats well below maintenance for a few weeks to reduce body fat, usually between longer bulking phases. A Grokipedia summary describes them as lasting about 2 to 6 weeks.
The same source says mini-cuts typically produce a few pounds of weight loss, much of it water and glycogen, and about 1 to 2 percent body fat reduction, with higher risks of muscle loss, fatigue and metabolic slowdown than a gradual cut. Wikipedia notes that larger deficits cause faster weight loss but a greater risk of losing muscle.
No clinical studies on mini-cuts were found.

name: Calorie counting

chain: Leaner or fuller face and body
angle.text: Looksmaxxers count calories to control cutting and bulking precisely, mainly to get lean enough to show facial and body definition. Tracking is a studied aid to weight change, while claims that it is the most reliable route to a leaner face are anecdotal.

summary: Logging every kilocalorie to cut or bulk; the standard tool for leanness, with eating-disorder caveats.
note: Studies have linked calorie tracking apps to eating-disorder symptoms in some users.
currentQuick:
Calorie counting means recording the energy in everything eaten to stay under or over a target. Looksmaxxers mostly use it to lose fat so the face looks leaner.
Research exists on weight management in general, but nothing measures facial appearance outcomes directly.
How it works: Energy values come from standard factors for protein, carbohydrate and fat, so logged numbers are estimates. Holding intake below expenditure produces weight loss; above it, weight gain.
Risks and caveats: One 2017 study found associations between calorie tracking and eating-disorder symptoms. Label values are estimates and can differ from absorbed energy.
deepLead:
Calorie counting is the practice of logging the energy content of everything eaten, usually in kilocalories and often with a phone app or food scale, in order to hold intake above or below a target. In looksmaxxing communities it is mainly used for fat loss ("cutting") to reveal facial and body leanness, and in reverse for deliberate weight gain.
Food energy figures come from the Atwater system, which multiplies measured protein, carbohydrate and fat by standard energy factors rather than burning food directly. Reference works note that this yields estimates, not exact values, and that labelled energy can differ from what a given person absorbs. Published research on tracking and weight management is mixed in focus: behavioural weight-management programmes have been meta-analysed, and some studies have examined links between calorie tracking and eating-disorder symptoms.

name: Macro tracking / IIFYM

angle.text: Lifters track macros, often under the flexible IIFYM approach, to drive cutting or bulking toward a defined physique. Protein and calorie targets are well studied; research on macro tracking itself as a method is limited.

summary: Tracking grams of protein, carbs and fat instead of just calories; common in cutting and bulking, little direct research.
note: No studies of IIFYM itself were found.
currentQuick:
Macro tracking means hitting daily targets for protein, carbs and fat. IIFYM is the flexible version where any food counts if the numbers fit.
It is a common method for gaining muscle or losing fat, but studies of IIFYM as such were not found.
How it works: Users log foods in an app against gram targets; total energy follows from standard energy factors per macronutrient.
Risks and caveats: Few direct risks are documented for the method itself. Experts disagree on ideal protein amounts, and logging accuracy depends on label estimates.
deepLead:
Macro tracking is the practice of logging daily grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat, rather than only total calories. "If It Fits Your Macros" (IIFYM) is the label for a flexible version in which any food is acceptable provided the targets are met. In looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is used to drive fat loss or muscle gain.
Sources available for this entry are thin. Bodybuilding reference material describes protein, carbohydrate and fat as the three macronutrients whose ratios vary with an individual's goals, and notes that experts disagree on ideal protein amounts. No clinical studies of IIFYM as a named approach were found.

name: Protein shakes / whey

angle.text: Users drink whey shakes to hit protein targets for muscle building and recovery, supporting a more muscular, leaner frame. Protein supplementation alongside training is well studied for muscle gain; no studies look at facial appearance.

summary: Milk-derived powder for hitting protein targets; about as effective as other protein sources, with no facial-appearance studies.
note: Whey is a milk-derived allergen for some people.
currentQuick:
Whey protein is a powder made from the liquid left over in cheese making, mixed into shakes for convenient protein. Lifters and looksmaxxers use it to support muscle gain and body composition.
A 2010 EFSA panel, as summarised in reference sources, found it roughly as effective as other proteins for muscle and strength.
How it works: Whey supplies amino acids that support muscle protein synthesis, especially after resistance exercise.
Risks and caveats: Whey can trigger milk allergy in some people. It is sold as a food supplement. Studies specific to appearance were not found.
deepLead:
Whey protein is a mixture of proteins isolated from whey, the liquid left when milk is curdled for cheese, and is sold as a powder for protein shakes. It is mainly used to meet protein targets for muscle building and recovery, which looksmaxxing communities link to body composition and a leaner, more muscular frame.
Reference sources report that the European Food Safety Authority in 2010 found no evidence supporting weight-loss claims for whey, and found it about as effective as other protein sources for strength, muscle and lean mass. Human trials listed in registries mostly study appetite, digestion, blood glucose and muscle function in older adults, not facial appearance.

name: Gallon of milk a day (GOMAD)

angle.text: GOMAD comes from strength circles and is discussed by looksmaxxers as a way to add mass quickly, for a bigger frame. It relies on the general link between a calorie surplus and weight gain; the named protocol itself has not been tested.

summary: A gallon of whole milk a day for a big calorie surplus; popular in strength circles, untested as a named method.
note: No studies of the method; large surpluses add body fat.
currentQuick:
GOMAD means drinking about a gallon of whole milk daily alongside meals to force weight gain. It comes from strength-training communities and is discussed by those wanting to bulk.
No studies of it as a named method were found.
How it works: Milk adds a large amount of calories and protein, producing a calorie surplus.
Risks and caveats: Reference material on bulking notes bigger surpluses add more fat. Dairy is a trigger for people with milk allergy or lactose intolerance.
deepLead:
GOMAD, short for "gallon of milk a day", is a weight-gain method from strength-training communities in which a lifter drinks roughly a gallon of whole milk daily on top of regular meals to create a large calorie surplus. Looksmaxxing spaces discuss it as a way to add mass.
Little citable material exists for this entry. Bodybuilding reference material describes bulking as eating a calorie surplus, notes that larger surpluses add more body fat, and lists dairy among high-protein foods. No clinical studies of GOMAD were found.

name: Big dirty bulk (Fast-food bulking)

angle.text: Users eat a very large surplus of calorie-dense fast food to gain mass quickly, planning to cut fat afterward. Faster scale gains are reported by lifters; comparisons with cleaner bulks rest mostly on anecdote.

summary: Eating a huge surplus of junk food to gain mass fast; faster gains reported, but more fat to cut afterward.
note: Reference sources mention heart-health and insulin-sensitivity concerns.
currentQuick:
A dirty bulk means eating a big calorie surplus without careful tracking, often from fast food. Proponents find it simpler than strict meal planning.
Bodybuilding references say it can speed gains but adds significant fat.
How it works: A large calorie surplus supplies energy for muscle growth, with excess stored as fat.
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns include added body fat requiring a harder cut and possible effects on heart health and insulin sensitivity.
deepLead:
A dirty bulk is a weight-gain approach in which a person eats a large calorie surplus without carefully tracking macronutrients, often using calorie-dense convenience or fast food. It contrasts with a "clean bulk" that aims to gain muscle with little fat.
Bodybuilding reference material says dirty bulking can speed muscle and strength gains but usually adds significant body fat, requiring a harder cut afterward, and mentions possible effects on heart health and insulin sensitivity. It also notes some lifters find it psychologically easier because it avoids strict meal planning and tracking. No clinical studies of fast-food bulking for appearance were found.

name: Eating for jaw (chewing hard foods)

angle.text: Users chew tough foods hoping to enlarge the masseters and sharpen the jawline, alongside mastic gum and jaw exercisers. The masseter can enlarge with heavy chewing, but hard-food diets themselves have not been tested for visible jaw change.

summary: Chewing tough foods to grow the masseter; the muscle can enlarge with heavy chewing, but hard-food diets are untested.
note: Overuse of the jaw is associated with TMJ problems in reference material.
currentQuick:
Eating for jaw means chewing hard, chewy foods to build the masseter and define the jawline.
The masseter can enlarge with habitual clenching or gum chewing, but no studies test hard-food diets for looks.
How it works: Repeated loading of the jaw-closing muscles may enlarge them, as seen with bruxism and constant gum chewing.
Risks and caveats: Reference material links masseter enlargement to facial asymmetry and temporomandibular joint problems.
deepLead:
Eating for jaw is the practice of regularly chewing tough or hard foods in the hope of enlarging the masseter and sharpening the jawline. It is discussed in looksmaxxing communities alongside mastic gum and jaw exercisers.
The masseter is one of the muscles of mastication and can enlarge in people who habitually clench or grind their teeth or chew gum, typically painlessly and sometimes asymmetrically. No studies were found testing hard-food diets for facial appearance.

name: Low-carb to lose face puffiness

angle.text: People go low-carb, sometimes briefly before a photo or event, to drop water weight and look leaner in the face. The shift in glycogen-bound water is well described; face-specific results have not been studied.

summary: Cutting carbs to drop glycogen-bound water and look leaner in the face; the water shift is well described, face-specific results are untested.
note: Low-carb diets have documented adverse effects in some groups; faster early weight loss is largely water.
currentQuick:
Some people in looksmaxxing communities cut carbohydrates for days or weeks before photos or events because they believe it makes the face look less puffy and more defined. The idea rests on the fact that stored carbohydrate (glycogen) is held in the body together with water.
Published research describes the glycogen-water link and the short-term weight changes of low-carb diets, but no study has measured facial puffiness or facial appearance after carbohydrate restriction.
How it works: Glycogen in muscle and liver is stored with roughly three to four parts water per part glycogen. When carbohydrate intake falls, glycogen stores drop and the associated water is lost, which is why early weight loss on low-carb diets is often described as largely water. Proponents extend this to the face; that extension has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: Low-carb diets are linked in reviews to side effects such as constipation, headache, bad breath, cramps and weakness, and rarely ketoacidosis. Persistent facial swelling can also have medical causes (kidney, heart, thyroid or allergic conditions), and clinicians advise that sudden swelling be evaluated.
deepLead:
Using a low-carbohydrate diet to reduce facial puffiness is a practice discussed in looksmaxxing and physique communities in which people restrict carbohydrates, sometimes briefly before a photo or event, in the belief that this reduces water retention and sharpens facial features. It is usually framed as a short-term appearance tactic rather than a long-term diet.
The physiological premise is that glycogen is stored in hydrated form, with about three to four parts water per part glycogen, so depleting glycogen releases water . Reviews of low-carbohydrate diets generally find little difference in fat loss compared with other diets when calories are matched . No published study has examined facial puffiness or facial appearance as an outcome of carbohydrate restriction.
